title: Language Effects: Figurative Language, Tone and Mood
summary: Every language device you meet in Checkpoint 6 reading, one method for any effect question, and the full list of effects you can write for each device.

blocks.text: What this page is about

In both Checkpoint reading sections (Paper 1 Non-fiction and Paper 2 Fiction, **Section A Reading, 25 marks each**), some questions ask about the **writer's language**: a simile, a metaphor, a rhetorical question, a comparison, one powerful word, or the tone of a passage. These questions are not asking **what** the writer used. They are asking **why** the writer used it and **what it does to the reader**.

This page teaches you every language device you need at Stage 6, one method that works for all of them, and the full list of effects you can write for each device. Learn the lists. In the exam you choose the effect that fits the text in front of you.

rows: A tool the writer uses on purpose, e.g. a simile or alliteration.
Words that do not mean exactly what they say, e.g. 'The classroom was a zoo.'
The real, everyday meaning of the words.
What the choice does to the reader: what they picture, feel, notice or expect.
Words that make a picture (or sound, smell, taste, feeling) in the reader's mind.
The writer's or narrator's attitude: how they 'sound' (angry, cheerful, worried).
The feeling the reader gets from the passage (tense, peaceful, gloomy).

blocks.text: The 4-step method for every effect question

items: **Step 1: Find it.** Go to the exact line or paragraph in the question. Underline the device or word.
**Step 2: Name it (only if asked).** Simile, metaphor, personification... Naming alone usually earns little or nothing.
**Step 3: Say what it makes the reader picture or feel.** This is where the marks are. Use: 'This makes the reader picture...', 'This creates a feeling of...', 'This shows that...'.
**Step 4: Prove it.** Quote a short, exact piece (one word to a few words) and make sure your explanation is about those words.

rows: 'The simile “as cold as a fish” makes the reader feel how unfriendly and unwelcoming the man was.'
'“The wind screamed” makes the wind sound like a frightened or angry person, so the storm feels wild and frightening.'
'The repeated ‘s’ in “soft, silver sand” sounds gentle and calm, so the beach feels peaceful.'

blocks.title: The vague-answer trap
items: 'It makes it interesting.' This is too vague: it could be said about any text in the world.
'It makes you want to read on.' This is only acceptable if you say WHAT the reader wants to find out.
'It creates a good image.' Say WHAT image: 'It makes the reader picture the river as a shiny silver ribbon.'
Test: could you have written your answer without reading this text? If yes, make it more specific.

blocks.title: سر الدرجة الكاملة في أسئلة التأثير

اكتب دائمًا: This makes the reader picture... أو This creates a feeling of...
اقتبس كلمة أو كلمتين فقط من النص بين علامتي تنصيص، واشرح هذه الكلمات نفسها.

blocks.text: Simile
A **simile** compares two different things using **'like'** or **'as'**. The writer wants you to see one thing through the picture of another.
**How to spot it:** look for 'like', 'as ... as' or 'as if' joining two different things. Careful: 'I like pizza' is not a simile (no comparison).
**Example:** 'The old bus rattled down the hill like a box of spoons.'

blocks.title: Why does the writer use a simile in line X? All the effects you can write
items: It helps the reader **picture** the thing clearly by comparing it with something familiar.
It **exaggerates** a quality (size, speed, noise, colour) so it stands out.
It shows the **character's feelings** (e.g. 'my heart was like a drum' shows fear or excitement).
It creates a **mood** (a frightening comparison creates fear, a gentle one creates calm).
It makes a **description more vivid and memorable** than a plain adjective would.
It can add **humour** when the comparison is funny or surprising.
In non-fiction, it explains a **difficult idea** by comparing it with something everyday (e.g. 'the heart works like a pump').

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text: 'Amir's hands shook like leaves in a storm as he waited for his name to be called.' Question: Why does the writer use a simile here? (2 marks)
**Full-mark answer:** The simile 'like leaves in a storm' makes the reader picture Amir's hands shaking fast and wildly. This shows how nervous and frightened he is while he waits.
**Why it scores:** One mark for the picture (shaking fast, out of control) and one mark for what it shows (his nervousness), with a short exact quotation.
Metaphor
A **metaphor** says one thing **is** another thing, without 'like' or 'as'. It is a stronger comparison than a simile because the writer does not say 'it is like'. The writer says 'it is'.
**How to spot it:** something is described as a different thing that it cannot really be: 'The playground was a battlefield.' The playground is not really a battlefield.
**Example:** 'After the rain, the road was a mirror.'

blocks.title: Why does the writer use a metaphor in line X? All the effects you can write
items: It makes the comparison **stronger and more direct** than a simile.
It helps the reader **picture** the thing (a road shining like glass).
It shows how a **character sees or feels** about something ('My room is my castle' shows he feels safe and in control there).
It **exaggerates** to show how extreme something is ('The test was a mountain' shows it felt huge and hard).
It creates a **mood** (a 'battlefield' playground feels noisy, rough and dangerous).
It packs a lot of meaning into **few words**.

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text: 'For Nour, the library was a treasure chest.' Question: Explain what the metaphor tells us about Nour. (2 marks)

**Full-mark answer:** Calling the library 'a treasure chest' suggests it is full of precious, exciting things to discover. This shows that Nour loves books and feels excited every time she goes there.
**Why it scores:** Explains the literal picture (precious things to find) and links it to Nour's feelings, with the exact phrase quoted.
Personification
**Personification** gives human actions, feelings or qualities to something that is not human: an object, an animal, the weather or an idea.
**How to spot it:** look for a non-human thing doing a human action: whispering, sighing, groaning, dancing, smiling, crying, complaining.
**Example:** 'The old door groaned as we pushed it open.'

blocks.title: Why does the writer use personification in line X? All the effects you can write
items: It makes the object seem **alive**, so the scene feels more real and vivid.
It creates a **mood**: a 'groaning' door feels creepy and **frightening**, 'dancing' leaves feel **happy and lively**.
It makes the setting feel **threatening** or **friendly**, depending on the action chosen.
It helps the reader **picture the movement or hear the sound** ('the wind whispered' = soft sound).
It can reflect the **character's feelings** (a nervous character notices 'the trees reaching for him').
It builds **tension or suspense** when the setting seems to be watching or attacking the character.

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text: 'All night, the angry storm punched at the windows.' Question: What is the effect of the word 'punched'? (2 marks)
**Full-mark answer:** 'Punched' makes the storm sound like an angry person hitting the house with their fists. This makes the storm seem violent and frightening, as if it is trying to break in.
**Why it scores:** Shows the picture (an angry person attacking the house) and the feeling it creates (fear, danger).
Alliteration
**Alliteration** is when words close together **start with the same sound**.

**How to spot it:** read the phrase aloud and listen to the first sounds: 'big, brave and bold'. It is the sound, not the letter, that counts: 'cute kitten' is alliteration (both words start with a 'k' sound).
**Example:** 'The slippery, slimy snake slid silently away.'

blocks.title: Why does the writer use alliteration in line X? All the effects you can write
items: It makes the phrase **memorable and catchy** (very common in headlines, adverts and slogans).
It **draws attention** to the words and the idea in them.
Soft sounds (s, l, m, f) create a **calm, gentle or quiet** mood, or a sly, secret feeling.
Hard sounds (b, d, k, t, p, g) create a **harsh, loud, angry or dramatic** effect.
It creates a **rhythm** that makes the text enjoyable to read aloud.
It can **imitate the sound** of the thing described (repeated 's' = hissing snake).
It can add **humour** or a playful tone.

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text (a headline): 'Brave Boys Beat the Big Freeze'. Question: Why does the writer use alliteration in the headline? (1 mark)
**Full-mark answer:** The repeated 'b' sound makes the headline catchy and memorable, so it grabs the reader's attention and makes them want to read the article.
**Why it scores:** For a headline, 'grabs attention' is accepted because the answer explains how (catchy and memorable).
Onomatopoeia
**Onomatopoeia** is a word that **sounds like the noise it describes**: buzz, crash, sizzle, splash, crunch, hiss, bang, drip, whoosh.
**How to spot it:** say the word aloud. If saying it copies the sound, it is onomatopoeia.
**Example:** 'Crunch, crunch went the frozen leaves under his boots.'

blocks.title: Why does the writer use onomatopoeia in line X? All the effects you can write
items: It helps the reader **hear** the sound, so the scene feels **real and alive**.
It puts the reader **inside the moment**, as if they are there.
A sudden loud word (BANG! CRASH!) creates **shock, surprise or drama**.
Quiet sounds (drip, tick, creak) can build **suspense and tension** in a silent scene.
Repeated sounds (tick... tick...) can show **time passing slowly** or the character's nerves.
It can make writing **lively, fun or funny** (often in children's stories and comics).

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text: 'Drip. Drip. Drip. The tap was the only sound in the dark kitchen.' Question: How does the writer create tension in this line? (2 marks)

**Full-mark answer:** The onomatopoeia 'Drip. Drip. Drip.' makes the reader hear one small, slow sound in the silence. This makes the kitchen feel very quiet and still, so the reader waits nervously for something to happen.
**Why it scores:** Names the choice, explains the sound picture and links it to the tension (waiting).
Hyperbole (exaggeration)
**Hyperbole** is a big **exaggeration** that is not meant to be taken literally.
**How to spot it:** ask: is this really possible? 'I've told you a million times', 'My bag weighs a ton', 'I was so hungry I could eat a horse.'
**Example:** 'This is the longest queue in the history of the world!'

blocks.title: Why does the writer use hyperbole in line X? All the effects you can write
items: It **emphasises** a feeling or quality (how hungry, how tired, how big).
It shows how **strongly** the character or writer feels.
It adds **humour** and makes the writing lively.
In persuasive writing, it makes something sound **amazing** (advert) or **terrible** (complaint) to persuade the reader.
It creates an **informal, chatty tone** (common in blogs, diaries and speech).

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text (a diary): 'The maths homework took about a hundred years.' Question: What does this line show about the writer's feelings? (1 mark)
**Full-mark answer:** The exaggeration shows that the writer found the homework very long and boring.
**Why it scores:** The 1-mark answer needs only the feeling (bored/fed up) linked to the exaggeration.
Imagery and the five senses

**Imagery** is description that makes a picture in the reader's mind. Good writers do not only describe what we **see**. They use all five senses. When you are asked how a writer makes a setting feel real, look for each sense.

rows: Helps the reader picture the scene, colours and light.
'Car horns argued in the street below.'
Makes the place feel busy, noisy or alive.
'The warm smell of fresh bread drifted from the bakery.'
Makes the place feel welcoming, homely, real.
'The sea air left salt on his lips.'
Puts the reader in the character's body, very close to the experience.
Lets the reader feel the pain, cold, heat or texture.

blocks.title: Why does the writer use imagery / sensory description? All the effects
items: It helps the reader **picture** the setting or character clearly.
It makes the scene feel **real**, as if the reader is **there**.
It creates a **mood or atmosphere** (cosy, eerie, busy, peaceful).
It shows the **character's feelings** through what they notice.
It slows the story down so the reader **notices an important moment**.
In non-fiction (travel writing, adverts), it makes a place or product sound **attractive** and persuades the reader.

blocks.text: Repetition
**Repetition** is when a word, phrase or sentence pattern is used more than once on purpose. It is different from careless repetition in your own writing: the writer chose it.
**Example:** 'We waited. We waited all morning. We waited until the sun was high.'

blocks.title: Why does the writer use repetition? All the effects
items: It **emphasises** the key word or idea so the reader remembers it.
It shows how **long** something lasted or how **slowly** time passed ('we waited... we waited').
It shows a character's strong **feeling** (worry, excitement, anger).
It builds **tension**, step by step, towards a big moment.
It creates a **rhythm**, especially in poems and speeches.
In persuasive writing, it **drives the message home** and makes it hard to forget ('We need trees. We need shade. We need clean air.').

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text: 'She checked the bag again. Again. And again.' Question: What does the repetition of 'again' show about the girl? (1 mark). **Answer:** It shows that she is very worried she has forgotten something, so she cannot stop checking.
Rhetorical questions

A **rhetorical question** is a question asked for effect. The writer does not expect an answer, or the answer is obvious. It is very common in persuasive texts, speeches, adverts, blogs and magazine articles (Paper 1), and sometimes in a narrator's thoughts (Paper 2).
**Example:** 'Who wants to breathe dirty air every day?'

blocks.title: Why does the writer use a rhetorical question? All the effects
items: It **speaks directly to the reader** and makes them feel involved.
It makes the reader **stop and think** about the issue.
It **persuades**: the answer is obvious, so the reader agrees with the writer ('No one wants that!').
It **introduces the topic** of a paragraph and makes the reader curious to read the answer.
It creates a **friendly, chatty tone** in a blog or article.
In a story, it shows the **character's confusion, worry or thoughts** ('What was that noise?').
It can build **suspense**, because the reader wants to find out the answer too.

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text (a leaflet): 'Would you leave your pet alone in a hot car? Of course not.' Question: Why does the writer begin with a question? (2 marks). **Answer:** The rhetorical question speaks directly to the reader and makes them imagine the situation. Because the answer is obviously 'no', the reader already agrees with the writer before the leaflet gives its advice.
Comparison and contrast

Sometimes a question asks about a **comparison** that is not a simile or metaphor: the writer puts two things side by side. Examples: 'The new park is twice as big as the old one.' / 'Outside, the street was roaring. Inside, the library was silent.' The effect is to make the difference **clear and striking**: the reader notices how big, how quiet, how much better or worse something is.
Other devices you may meet

rows: Words chosen to make the reader feel strong emotion
Makes the reader feel sorry, angry or worried, so they are persuaded.
Surprises the reader and makes the strange feeling stand out.
Same vowel sound repeated inside nearby words
Creates a slow, smooth sound or rhythm.
Sounds calm and gentle, or sly and secret.
An object that stands for a bigger idea
Adds a deeper meaning to the story.
A joke using a word with two meanings
Adds humour, often in headlines and adverts.
Makes the text personal and involving.

blocks.text: The effect of a single word (word choice)

Many 1- and 2-mark questions ask about **one word**: 'What does the word “stomped” suggest about how Sam was feeling?' or 'Why has the writer chosen the word “crept”?' The writer picked that word instead of a plain one. Your job is to say what **extra meaning** it gives.

items: **Quote** the word.
**Compare** it with a plain word in your head (stomped vs walked).
**Say what extra meaning** it adds: how it was done, what it shows about feelings, what picture or mood it creates.

rows: quietly and carefully, maybe afraid of being heard
secret, scared or careful not to wake someone
looked closely, trying hard to see something unclear
extremely small, maybe weak or easy to miss

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text: 'Huda snatched the letter from the table.' Question: What does the word 'snatched' suggest about Huda? (1 mark). **Answer:** It suggests she took the letter quickly and suddenly because she was desperate (or worried) to read it before anyone else.

blocks.title: Positive or negative?
blocks.text: Many words carry a feeling (connotation). 'Slim' sounds positive, 'skinny' sounds less kind. 'Curious' sounds positive, 'nosy' sounds negative. If a question asks what a word shows about the writer's opinion, check whether the word sounds positive or negative.
Tone and mood
These two are often mixed up, but they answer different questions.

blocks.title: How to answer a tone or mood question
items: Choose a **precise** word: not 'good' or 'bad' but 'tense', 'nostalgic', 'cheerful'.
Give **evidence**: quote the words that create the tone or mood.
Explain **how** those words create it: 'The dark corridor and the creaking floor create a tense mood because the reader expects something to jump out.'
Watch for a **change** in tone or mood (calm at the start, frightening at the end). Questions often ask about the change.

blocks.text: **Worked mini-example.** Text: 'The beach was empty. Grey waves crashed against the rocks and a cold wind pulled at the abandoned umbrellas.' Question: What mood does the writer create? Give one quotation. (2 marks). **Answer:** A gloomy, lonely mood (1). The 'grey waves' and 'abandoned umbrellas' make the beach seem cold, empty and sad (1).

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: Naming the device and stopping there.
Writing a vague effect ('it makes it interesting').
Quoting a whole sentence when one or two words were enough.
Calling 'like' a simile when nothing is being compared ('She looked like she was tired' is not a real comparison).
Mixing up tone (the writer's attitude) and mood (the reader's feeling).
Giving one idea for a 2-mark question.
Explaining a different word from the one in the question.

blocks.text: Checklist before you answer

items: I went to the exact line or paragraph.
I quoted a short, exact piece of evidence.
I said what the reader pictures, hears or feels.
I linked it to the character, mood, or the writer's purpose.
My answer could only be about THIS text.
I gave enough points for the marks.

blocks.text: Practice questions
Read each short original text and answer. Then open the answer and compare. The explanation shows what earns the mark.

items.q: 'The fog wrapped the village in a thick grey blanket.' (a) Name the device. (b) What effect does it create? (2 marks)
items.a: (a) Metaphor (the fog is called a blanket) and personification (the fog 'wrapped' the village) are both accepted. (b) It makes the reader picture the fog as thick and heavy, covering everything so nothing can be seen. It creates a quiet, closed-in mood.

items.q: 'Rami was as quiet as a mouse when the head teacher walked in.' Why does the writer use a simile here? (2 marks)
items.a: The simile 'as quiet as a mouse' makes the reader picture Rami keeping completely still and silent (1). It shows that he felt nervous or afraid of the head teacher and did not want to be noticed (1).

items.q: 'Sizzle! The eggs hit the hot pan.' Give one effect of the word 'Sizzle!'. (1 mark)
items.a: It is onomatopoeia: it lets the reader hear the eggs cooking, so the moment feels real, as if they are in the kitchen. (Also accepted: it makes the opening sudden and lively.)

items.q: 'The mountain watched over the little town.' What does the word 'watched' suggest? (1 mark)
items.a: Personification: it suggests the mountain is like a guardian protecting the town, so the town feels safe. (If the story is frightening, 'the mountain is spying on the town' can also be accepted. Always link to the mood of the text.)

items.q: Headline: 'Super Sam Saves Stranded Seal'. Why has the writer used alliteration? (1 mark)
items.a: The repeated 's' sound makes the headline catchy and memorable, so it grabs the reader's attention.

items.q: 'I have explained this a thousand times!' shouted Dad. What does the hyperbole show about Dad? (1 mark)
items.a: It shows that Dad is very frustrated and annoyed because he feels he has explained it many times already.

items.q: Leaflet: 'Do you want your child to be safe on the road? Then read on.' Give two reasons why the writer uses a rhetorical question. (2 marks)
items.a: Any two: it speaks directly to the parent and makes them feel involved / it makes them stop and think about their child's safety / the answer is obviously 'yes', so they agree with the writer / it makes them curious to read the advice.

items.q: 'Click. Click. Click. The lights would not come on.' How does the writer create tension? (2 marks)
items.a: The repeated onomatopoeia 'Click' makes the reader hear the switch being pressed again and again with no result (1). This shows the character's growing panic in the dark and makes the reader wait anxiously for what will happen next (1).

items.q: 'Grandma's kitchen smelled of cinnamon and warm honey.' Which sense does the writer appeal to, and what mood is created? (2 marks)
items.a: Smell (1). It creates a warm, cosy, welcoming mood, as if the kitchen is a safe, happy place (1).

items.q: 'Lina tiptoed past her brother's room.' Why does the writer use 'tiptoed' instead of 'walked'? (1 mark)
items.a: 'Tiptoed' shows Lina is moving very quietly and carefully because she does not want her brother to hear or wake up.

items.q: Choose the best word for the tone: 'Brilliant. The bus is late again. What a perfect start to my day.' A) grateful B) sarcastic C) calm D) admiring (1 mark)
items.a: B) sarcastic. The writer says 'brilliant' and 'perfect' but means the opposite: they are annoyed that the bus is late.

items.q: 'The classroom was a beehive before the bell.' Explain the metaphor. (2 marks)
items.a: The classroom is compared to a beehive (1). This makes the reader picture lots of children moving around busily and hear a loud buzzing noise of talking, so the room seems noisy and full of energy (1).

items.q: 'Danger. Danger everywhere. Danger in the water, danger in the trees.' What is the effect of the repetition? (2 marks)
items.a: Repeating 'danger' emphasises how unsafe the place is (1) and builds tension, making the reader feel the character is surrounded with no safe place to go (1).

items.q: 'The streets were silent. Not a single car passed. Only the wind moved the dry leaves.' What mood is created? Support with a quotation. (2 marks)
items.a: A lonely, eerie (or tense) mood (1). Quotation: 'The streets were silent' / 'Not a single car passed'. The empty streets make the place feel strange and abandoned (1).

items.q: Article: 'Plastic bags kill thousands of helpless sea turtles every year.' Which word is emotive, and why is it used? (2 marks)
items.a: 'helpless' (also accept 'kill') (1). It makes the reader feel sorry for the turtles and angry about plastic, so they are persuaded to stop using plastic bags (1).

items.q: 'The sun was a golden coin in the sky.' Is this a simile or a metaphor? Explain how you know. (1 mark)
items.a: A metaphor: it says the sun IS a golden coin, without using 'like' or 'as'.

items.q: 'The car roared up the hill.' What two things does 'roared' suggest? (2 marks)
items.a: Any two: the car is very loud / it is powerful / it is going fast / it sounds like a fierce animal, which makes it seem strong or frightening.

items.q: Story opening: 'Everything was perfect. The sun was shining, the birds were singing, and nobody guessed what would happen at three o'clock.' How does the mood change? (2 marks)
items.a: It starts happy and peaceful ('the sun was shining, the birds were singing') (1) but changes to tense and mysterious with 'nobody guessed what would happen', which warns the reader something bad is coming (1).
